passages.label: A
passages.text: What would it be like to inspect a spacecraft in the same room as your desk? NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory developed Spacecraft AR to superimpose a digital model on the image from a mobile camera, and the screen shows a viewpoint that can change as the user moves. This technique takes a machine from the domain of space engineering and gives students an engaging way to manipulate a model and observe parts from several angles.

passages.label: B
passages.text: A user first finds a clear, flat surface and selects a mission from categories including Earth, Mars, Planetary, Launch and Other. The menu includes numerous explorers, among them Perseverance, Cassini, Voyager, the International Space Station and Landsat 9, and the app can display a model at tabletop size or in true-to-life proportions. Users can move the model across the floor, change its size and walk around it, and these controls allow them to manipulate a representation rather than study one fixed image, and they can also take pictures of the spacecraft in their own surroundings.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The two display settings serve different purposes, and a small model makes the whole craft easy to inspect, and it makes the overall design visible, while a life-size display can reveal how large a rover, satellite or antenna would feel beside a person. NASA also supplies mission information and animated movement. Together, these features supplement a conventional diagram, and a teacher might ask learners to compare solar panels, instruments or landing systems and explain how a shape relates to a mission. Students can rotate a craft, pause their viewing and return to a detail, so one shared model can support both individual noticing and group explanation. The experience can be immersive without hiding the real room, because the digital model and the learner's environment remain visible together.

passages.label: D
passages.text: A model can simulate structure but leave an imperfect impression of texture or scale, and a student unfamiliar with the controls might ask a peer to verify which part they are looking at. A label that appears illegible from one angle can be seen more easily from another, while superfluous labels may obscure where pieces connect. It would be inefficient to repeat the same view if a drawing can supply it more clearly. The model is insufficient for checking measurements, and a photograph or mission diagram can be indispensable when a learner has to explain where the evidence came from. The changing viewpoint is an aid to spatial interpretation, especially when perspective or lighting in a single photograph could obscure the relationship between two components. A labelled dimension supplies different evidence, especially if a change of scale obscures the original proportion, and an enlarged projection may exaggerate an attachment or conceal a gap between separate components, so the scale needs to be clear.

passages.label: E
passages.text: The novelty of an immersive view can attract attention, and an educational aid still has to support a clear question, such as whether a flat projection hides a feature on the far side. Numerous views can help, but an interpretation of how a part works may depend on labels or other evidence. A teacher might suggest that students use the model to supplement a diagram, then ask whether they can claim that a particular feature is visible. The activity makes the model useful beyond its first appearance on the screen.

passages.label: A
passages.text: When technicians inspect an aircraft component, a specialist may need to observe a problem from another place. Ordinary video can show what a camera sees. Augmented reality adds an aid that can superimpose a mark on the view to identify a location, and the people need a shared interpretation of what the mark identifies, especially when simultaneous instructions concern parts close to one another. A marker can supplement a conversation in this domain, but a misleading pointer can also become a hazard.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Ordinary audio or video calls allowed people to talk, but they can limit the shared view of a physical task. Extended-reality systems can show both partners the same equipment and add visual information to that view, and a remote expert might point to a component, mark a location or guide an inspection while the local technician remains beside the equipment. The FAA report reviewed 74 research articles and grouped evidence by device types, interaction modes, evaluation measures and human-factors concerns. The studies did not all ask the same question, so their measures cannot simply be combined into one score, and this broad review helps readers interpret design patterns without treating every system as identical.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The local technician must verify how an annotation identifies equipment, since an illegible label or an imperfect camera view may be insufficient to establish a location. A peer can help simulate a maintenance task with an unfamiliar interface, allowing researchers to test whether superfluous instructions make communication inefficient and whether confirmation by audio is indispensable when interruptions are unavoidable. Those measurements can establish how accurate the shared interpretation is before a system is relied on in practice. A study can compare the accuracy of shared spatial alignment and distinguish delay in reporting from misidentification of a component.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Human factors can determine whether an additional display improves collaboration or creates a new hazard. Text can obstruct a technician's view, inaccurate registration can direct attention to the wrong component, and heavy equipment can cause fatigue, particularly when protective gear limits the use of controls. Teams also need to coordinate speech and visual annotations so that guidance reaches the right person at a usable moment. An interface designed for a demonstration may therefore need substantial changes before it supports reliable communication during real maintenance. A message that arrives after the inspection has moved on may be more of a risk than a help, even when the advice is clear and correct.

passages.label: E
passages.text: The evidence therefore supports cautious field evaluation, and researchers can compare task time, errors, workload, communication quality and the accuracy of shared understanding. A useful study should state who performed the task, what equipment was used and what counted as success, and it should not assert a general benefit from one demonstration. The reviewers conclude that extended reality can improve visualisation and shared perspective, while further human-factors studies and field evaluations are needed. Their review suggests a sequence of controlled trials followed by realistic workplace tests. This balanced interpretation keeps a promising tool connected to the safety rules and expert judgement that aviation maintenance already requires. An expert may manipulate an annotation while a colleague verifies what it identifies, and a researcher can claim a stronger result if the test measures errors as well as speed.

passages.label: A
passages.text: The Smithsonian's Bone Hall is a comparative-anatomy exhibition containing 300 vertebrate skeletons, and in 2015 the National Museum of Natural History released the Skin and Bones app to supplement cases. Thirteen animals received digital stories, and when a visitor pointed a device at a specimen, the app could place flesh, movement, or internal mechanisms over the bones. The designers intended an extension of the collection rather than a replacement for it, and the curatorial project examined whether augmented reality could connect old objects with an interpretive and interactive layer of digital visualisation.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The package contained ten AR experiences, 32 videos, and four activities, with fixed pieces brief and AR sequences lasting no more than one minute and four seconds. A three-dimensional model could be superimposed over a skeleton while tracking adjusted its orientation and size as the visitor moved, helping explain functional anatomy. Each digital projection depended on an unobstructed view of the chosen case, and an animation could, for example, show how a woodpecker's long tongue works. The app also used a repeated icon and visual instructions to indicate when an AR feature was available and how to frame the specimen.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Researchers investigated use in the hall, recruiting visitors randomly as they entered, either alone or in small groups, and including people over twelve. Participants received a research iPad without verbal instructions or an advance explanation of the app, making the test closer to a self-guided visit. The device recorded selected content and viewing duration, while researchers noted stops and behaviour before inviting visitors to complete a questionnaire or interview, gathering 199 questionnaires and 15 interviews over the 92 days of the study in 2015. The combination allowed them to compare what people did with accounts of their experience.

passages.label: D
passages.text: More than 90 per cent of participants reported feeling comfortable with technology, although previous exposure to museum augmented reality was limited. A user unfamiliar with the controls might ask a peer to verify which skeleton a display was meant to simulate. An illegible instruction or an imperfect camera view could cause delay, and a screen that supplies superfluous facts may be inefficient where visitors have time for a single exhibit. A brief stop is insufficient evidence of learning, while the physical specimens are irreplaceable for comparing the screen with the shapes on display. Activation failures accounted for 6.9 per cent of attempts, often following misidentification of a skeleton or insufficient distance from it. Most visitors viewed the display for one to five minutes, with a mean duration of eight minutes and ten seconds. This distinction matters because technical interruption can affect measured engagement independently of interest or comprehension. Recorded interactions distinguish technical availability from participation without treating every viewing time as equivalent.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Interpretation requires care when researchers observe numerous visitors using the app to inspect specimens, because an apparently engaging experience might reflect the novelty of an immersive display, or a chance to manipulate a virtual feature, instead of attention to the actual skeleton. Crowds, competing sound and inconsistent connectivity can also affect participation. To conclude that the application is an effective learning aid, an advocate would need evidence of what people could explain afterward. A follow-up question could suggest whether an animated projection helped a visitor identify the movement of a particular joint.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What would count as fulfilling the design aim in the opening?
options: Make people stop looking at the collection once their devices are on.
Use a digital example to explain a feature of a displayed skeleton while retaining the exhibit.
Move the old collection away so the digital stories become the only exhibits.
Avoid connecting the animations with anything people can see in the museum.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which detail helps explain why aiming a camera at the right place matters?
options: The model appears at the same size and orientation regardless of where the user moves.
Every available icon controls all the other specimens at once.
The recorded visit duration determines which part a visitor can see.
The projection needs a clear view of the chosen case to align with the specimen.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: How can the study approximate an ordinary visit while still collecting structured data?
options: Visitors could work out how to use the screen's prompts themselves, while the device and researchers recorded behaviour.
The screen displayed no help and all participants were shown the next action aloud.
Device records meant people could visit only in groups at the same starting time.
Participants had to follow the same steps before any data could be collected.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why did the researchers use records and questionnaires or interviews?
options: A questionnaire establishes the exact time of every selection without records.
An interview means no observation is needed for what visitors did.
The combination allows observed behaviour to be compared with people's accounts of their experience.
They give two different ways of recording only the app's activation failures.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why could a short visit and an unusually long visit both give the wrong impression about learning from the specimen?
options: Visit length itself shows who understands each part of the real object.
Only the visitor who took a short time could have experienced any distraction.
The shortest visits necessarily resulted from knowing all the information already, while the longest show interest only in real objects.
A technical problem can cut a visit short, while novelty can hold someone's attention without showing what they learned about the specimen.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why do the range most people spent and the reported mean need to be read separately?
options: The mean was the time spent by every visitor studied.
Most visits were in a shorter range than the mean, so the two figures describe the visit lengths differently.
The longer duration was the required minimum for an interview.
Each failed start was counted as eight minutes and ten seconds.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What does reported comfort with technology fail to establish?
options: That a person already knows how to use museum augmented reality or will avoid technical problems with it
Whether the collection has at least one physical model
That the study took place in a hall open to visitors
Whether any participant was allowed to select a feature

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What would help researchers distinguish trouble getting a feature to start from trouble understanding it once it is visible?
options: Count every attempt to activate a feature as evidence the visitor learned from it.
Use the total time for both questions and assume all delays are difficulty understanding the exhibit.
Record failed starts separately and ask a question about what users can explain after seeing the feature.
Replace the physical objects with a longer set of animations and count how many are available.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Two visitors spend similar time with the app, but one attended mainly to the animation and the other compared it with a real specimen. What would help distinguish their learning?
options: Treat the same length of use as proof the two people know the same things.
Use the records to see what each viewed and ask what feature of the actual specimen each can now explain.
Add another video and decide that its length explains all differences.
Assume a visitor who moved a virtual element necessarily understood its real counterpart.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which conclusion fits the article's account of the display and its evaluation?
options: Opening the app replaces the need to look at or explain any physical exhibit.
A longer recorded visit is enough to establish that a visitor understood all available features.
The app's attractiveness by itself verifies that it improves learning for every visitor.
Digital views can add to the exhibit, while judging learning requires evidence beyond activation, interest and viewing time.
